issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: 'Being followed or tracked' is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one and with the rest of the profile, which centers on grief, guilt, and generalized somatic alarm rather than a pursuit/persecution context. It stands apart from the other trigger items and does not connect plausibly to the memory content provided.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
issues.explanation: 'My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy' is not well aligned with the rest of the formulation and item set. The profile otherwise emphasizes guilt, grief, misery, fragmented/numb recall, and bodily false alarms after a loved-one trauma. A 'going crazy' appraisal is possible, but here it appears weakly supported by the trigger and memory content and feels clinically out of step relative to the otherwise bereavement/guilt-focused presentation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, severe guilt, misery, and a sense that life has been destroyed can be coherent. However, the specific appraisal 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is notably more global and suicidal in tone than the rest of the selected profile, and it is not supported by corresponding threat, memory, trigger, or strategy content. With the provided five components, this item stands out as insufficiently anchored to the rest of the formulation-relevant material, making the node less internally coherent.

vignette: Kai was twenty-two when his younger brother, Jett, died after a night at a coastal wedding reception. The celebration had grown restless, and Jett had argued with his friends about leaving early, only to step outside into the humid air, finish a beer standing up, and get behind the wheel of his truck. Kai had been across the yard, watching the string lights flicker, when his phone rang. He remembered the way the room seemed to tilt, the sharp scent of spilled lager on the wooden tables, and the sudden, violent collapse of everything he had counted on. When he arrived at the hospital, the nurses were still trying to explain that Jett's body had reacted before the mind could process what was coming. Kai left the scene before the paperwork was signed. The night never settled into a sequence he could follow. When he tried to hold the hours in his mind, a heavy guilt pressed against his ribs, sharp and suffocating. At other times, the memory came through completely numb, as if he were watching a film of someone else's life. His body, meanwhile, refused to wait for his thoughts. He would catch his shoulders tensing the moment a car backfired, or his breath catching when a delivery driver dropped a box. He was certain that his nervous system was still tracking threats that had already passed, and he often caught himself flinching at empty parking lots or startled by quiet phone notifications, certain that danger was closing in even when the street was empty. His muscles stayed wound tight, a perpetual readiness that left him exhausted by mid-afternoon. These experiences arrived without warning, overlapping in his daily routine, side by side. At twenty-four, Kai worked as a staff pharmacist at a busy downtown clinic. The dispensary floor became a landscape of quiet alarms. He was particularly sensitive to the scent of alcohol, a smell that had long been discouraged on the premises but still slipped through on a customer's coat or a coworker's breath during a hurried break. Each time the odor caught in his nose, his stomach dropped, and he would immediately step behind the double doors, hands trembling, certain he was seconds from another loss. He also found himself watching people in the waiting area with a sharp, unrelenting judgment. When a man loudly complained about insurance codes or a teenager fumbled with a prescription at the pickup counter, Kai's jaw tightened. He had come to believe that when people misbehaved, the world was slipping back toward that same careless edge. He avoided community funerals and would not walk past the cemetery on his commute, telling himself he simply needed time, though the distance between him and the grieving crowds only widened. His Pacific Islander family had always gathered around long tables, but now the prospect of another reunion felt unbearable. His life felt destroyed, stripped of the color it once held, and nothing in his work or his evenings carried weight. He kept the shelves stocked, counted vials with precise fingers, and answered questions in a calm voice, but inside he felt hollowed out. What frightened him most was the fear that he would never feel like himself again, that the grief and the tension would become his permanent furniture. The man he used to be, the one who laughed easily at staff meetings and planned weekend hikes with friends, felt like a stranger to him. He finally walked into the community mental health clinic on a Tuesday afternoon, clutching a referral slip he had printed from his phone. He did not know if talking would untangle the memory or quiet the constant hum in his chest, but he was hoping someone might help him figure out how to live without bracing for the next crash. He was tired of the false alarms, tired of the guilt that came and went without warning, and tired of watching his own life pass by through a pane of thick glass. He sat in the waiting room, smelling the faint antiseptic of the clinic, and waited to see if someone could help him piece together a story he could finally tell.
